newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish KGHM copper firm seen trading around PLN 21.
newsitem.headline: Polish KGHM copper firm seen trading around PLN 21.

text.p: Polish copper firm KGHM Polska Miedz SA, the world's fifth largest producer of electrolytic copper, should start trade on the Warsaw bourse on Thursday around its issue price of 21 zlotys, analysts said.

They said KGHM, whose 65-million-share public offering last week saw a greater oversubscription in its small-investor tranche, may then drift or fall as relatively few institutional investors were seen buying from profit-taking Poles.
Small investors bought 16 million KGHM shares at 19 zlotys.

Analysts said the firm compared unfavourably to many foreign copper stocks. Its 1996 price-earnings ratio of 19.1 at the previous 19.5-zloty minimum institutional issue price was already higher than the main Warsaw index's current 13.6,

"I don't think foreign investors will think it's worth it to buy higher because KGHM is a well valued firm and there's no discount to other firms as Handlowy had to other banks," said Aleksander Jawien, a trader at PBR brokerage.
Bank Handlowy, Poland's other high-profile privatisation this year, started trade only 8.3 percent above issue a week ago Monday but then rose for six straight sessions.
Analysts said some demand for KGHM could come from the institutional investors who were not allotted 8.8 million shares because they did not take part in book-building.
But analysts said that though KGHM shares might prove desirable to more general investment funds impressed by Poland's economic growth, mining funds might stay away.

"I think if there is demand it will be the sort of demand that looks at it and says 'blue chip stock in the Polish market, therefore buy it'," said Martin van Tol, an analyst at Raiffeisen Zentralbank in London.
The firm is selling 35 million shares in the offer as GDRs.
Analysts said KGHM's longer-term bourse price depended largely on copper prices, about which many were pessimistic.
"If you're really bullish on the price of copper you're going to want to further buy KGHM," said Remigiusz Tarka, an analyst at IB Austria Securities in Warsaw.
"But it seems the copper price will fall. There are lots of new investments in that industry, very large supply from cheap producers and demand is growing slower than supply," he added.

Analysts also questioned the feasibility of KGHM's plan to reduce costs 26 percent by the end of the decade, putting them around world levels, as the firm was an underground mine and had several open-cast competitors.
They also said KGHM, whose costs were in zlotys but earnings in dollars, was vulnerable to zloty appreciation.

"The current central bank policy is to depreciate and the current account deficit sort of points towards that at the moment, but a couple of years down the line...appreciation in real terms can't be ruled out," Raiffeisen's van Tol said.
